That early curiosity grew into a clear professional direction through my Bachelor’s degree at a university not listed in the major global rankings, where I built my understanding of mechanical systems and how sound design decisions affect efficiency, reliability, and performance. Through this, I have strengthened my research, teamwork, communication, organization, and ability to work under pressure. I consider myself dependable and thoughtful, and I am eager to build on this foundation in a Mechanical Engineer role.

A quiet comment at a community fundraiser has stayed with me ever since a relative turned to me and said, “Now I understand why everyone stops to talk to you.” That moment captured why social work feels so personal to me. I was drawn to this profession by a deep belief that timely support and compassionate advocacy can change the course of someone’s life, especially during moments of crisis or transition. What motivates me most is helping individuals and families feel heard, connected to resources, and empowered to move forward with dignity. Originally from Peru, I have built my academic and professional path around that commitment, completing a Master’s degree at a university ranked in the global top 500 and applying that learning in practice through projects that led to tangible outcomes, including one completed project with clear results.

Through my studies and practical experience, I have strengthened my understanding of person-centred support, assessment, and coordinated intervention. In one area of practice, I spent more than a year steadily learning a new case-management tool, using it regularly until I could work with it confidently in everyday tasks and use it to keep support plans accurate and up to date. In routine situations, I work carefully through established procedures to make sure referrals, records, and follow-up actions are handled properly; when an unusual case has required a response outside normal guidance, I have sought advice promptly so that decisions remained safe and appropriate. In addition, working alongside colleagues has shown me the value of dependable teamwork: when asked, I have shared what I knew about local resources and documentation steps to help others complete their work smoothly.

What continues to shape my approach is the opportunity to build trust quickly with people from diverse backgrounds, assess needs thoughtfully, and coordinate practical support that is realistic and focused on outcomes. Through this, I have developed strong organisation, communication, and collaborative working skills, while becoming more grounded in sensitive, structured practice. As a result, I am ready to contribute as a Social Worker and continue growing in a role centred on dignity, advocacy, and meaningful support.

Few professions shape daily life as visibly as civil engineering, and that is what first drew me in: the chance to help create bridges, roads, and public spaces that are resilient, practical, and genuinely useful to the communities they serve. That early fascination grew into a clear commitment to becoming a Civil Engineer, because the role brings together problem-solving, creativity, and public impact in a tangible way. I am from Spain and hold a Master’s degree from a university not listed in the major global rankings. Through that academic foundation, I developed my understanding of infrastructure design and delivery, and I completed 2 projects with tangible outcomes, experiences that showed me how technical requirements can be turned into practical, buildable solutions that balance safety, cost, and long-term performance. Beyond formal study, I spent more than a year steadily working with a new design and analysis tool until using it became part of my normal workflow, an experience that taught me the value of consistent practice when building technical capability.

Furthermore, in project settings I have learned the importance of dependable, methodical work. On routine design and coordination tasks, I follow established procedures carefully to resolve day-to-day issues, while on less familiar cases I make a point of checking details with senior engineers before moving forward. Working alongside colleagues has also been central to my development; for example, when a teammate asked how I had set up part of a drawing package and document trail, I walked them through my process so they could apply the same approach on their section of the work. This collaborative side of engineering is one of the reasons the profession feels so rewarding to me.

A moment that stays with me came on a family road trip when we crossed a bridge I had helped deliver. My relatives insisted on stopping for a photo and joked that it was the only holiday landmark where I could explain the drainage system in detail. Looking ahead, that memory captures exactly why I want this role: to contribute to infrastructure that people use every day and can rely on for years to come.
